title: AI-Assisted S-Parameter Prediction
description: High-speed interconnect evaluation depends on repeated signal analysis, which can make design exploration computationally expensive. For the TE AI Cup 2022-23, our Rutgers team developed neural-network architectures and signal preprocessing methods to predict IEEE-standard Channel Operating Margin (COM) parameters in place of a time-consuming model-based MATLAB workflow. The project received the Best AI Innovation prize. Rutgers estimated $12.5M in potential savings in tester time and capital expenditure for high-speed testing.

title: Ultra-Low-Power Analog Neural Networks for ECG Monitoring
description: Continuous ECG analysis requires inference within tight power and hardware budgets. This research investigates analog folded neural networks, reusing computation resources over time rather than allocating separate hardware to every operation. The work spans resistive processing units, analog activation functions, and hybrid analog-digital sensing architectures. The engineering focus is the tradeoff among inference capability, circuit complexity, and power consumption for wearable health-monitoring applications.

title: Spiking Neural Networks for Signal Processing
description: Always-on sensing must extract useful information from time-varying inputs within a limited energy budget. This research examines spiking neural networks and hybrid analog-digital implementations for IoT sensing and smart-camera applications. The work focuses on temporal representations and event-driven computation, assessing how neural architecture and hardware implementation affect the cost of continuous signal processing.

title: Full-Duplex Underwater Acoustic Communications
description: Full-duplex underwater acoustic links must recover incoming signals while suppressing interference from their own transmitter. This research addresses that constraint through spatial self-interference cancellation, supported by work on joint Doppler estimation and compensation. The objective is to improve acoustic-channel utilization while accounting for the propagation and motion effects that complicate underwater communications. The project connects signal-processing methods with experimental acoustic-link evaluation.
